why-title.2: Plenty of tools let you run several agents side by side. Pyloxa handles what happens between them: who does which part, how you know it is done, and who takes over when one gets stuck.
why-title.3: Here is the same request three ways: switching between CLIs yourself, putting several agent terminals side by side in a terminal multiplexer, and handing it to Pyloxa.
why-title.9: You decide which tool fits each part and paste the request over.
why-title.11: You decide what the agent in each terminal does; some tools also let an agent start helper agents.
why-title.12: The brain breaks the request into phases and tasks and routes each one by your rules, naming the rule it matched.
why-title.15: When one agent finishes, you paste the API shape and file paths into the next.
why-title.17: Agents can message each other; what gets handed over is up to the agents.
why-title.18: The next phase receives a handoff package: the results, the checks that passed, and what to watch for.
why-title.21: The agent says it is done, and you run the tests to find out.
why-title.23: You see which agents are working, done or waiting for you; whether the result is right is still yours to check.
why-title.24: A task is done when your verification commands pass in its own worktree. If they fail, the agent gets one automatic fix. You can also have a different agent write tests for it and the brain review it; the brain's verdict is labelled as an AI review.
why-title.27: You switch tools and explain again where things stand.
why-title.29: That terminal stops and waits; arranging a takeover is up to you.
why-title.30: Pyloxa proposes the fallback from your rules; once you confirm, it continues from the files the first agent changed.
why-title.33: The agent edits your working directory directly.
why-title.35: Depends on how you open the terminal; usually your working directory.
why-title.36: Every task works in its own git worktree, and its changes are checked against the allowed write scope. Merging and pushing stay your call.
why-title.41: Watching many terminals at once, keeping agents running even after you quit the app, or working on remote machines.
why-title.42: Splitting one request across agents and checking the results before they are merged.
supervised-title.1: Not a platform where agents run themselves
supervised-title.2: Some platforms let agents run like a company: assigning their own work, waking up on a schedule and running around the clock. Pyloxa takes the other road. Agents do only what you ask, and their results are checked before you merge them.
supervised-title.4: Runs directly on Windows 10 and 11. No WSL, no Docker, and no server or database to set up.
supervised-title.6: An agent saying it's done doesn't count. Pyloxa runs the verification commands you approved in the task's own worktree, and the task is done when they pass.
supervised-title.8: Pyloxa never uses modes that skip every permission check, such as --dangerously-skip-permissions. Changes outside the allowed write scope are never accepted automatically.
supervised-title.10: Pyloxa never reads, copies or sends CLI credentials, and never shares your subscription with anyone. Agents run on the official CLIs you signed in to.
supervised-title.12: Agents work only on what you asked for and never create work of their own. When quota runs out, work stops or hands over by your rules.
supervised-title.13: A verification card for your PR
supervised-title.14: When you open a PR, you can attach a verification card: which commands actually ran, who cross-tested, and how each result was accepted.

faq-title.3: Pyloxa is a desktop app for Windows 10 and 11 that gets AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex CLI to work together. You describe the work once, and the brain splits it into tasks and hands each one to a CLI by your routing rules. Every task runs in its own git worktree and is checked with your verification commands, and you decide what gets merged. If one CLI runs out of quota, another takes over once you confirm. Pyloxa uses your own subscriptions or API keys. The free edition needs no account; Pro, US$79 a year, adds running several projects at once, auto mode and automatic fallback, and is in a free preview now: sign in to use it.
faq-title.4: Does Pyloxa charge for AI usage?
faq-title.5: No. Pyloxa runs the official CLIs you already set up (Claude Code, Codex CLI and, experimentally, Gemini CLI), so usage counts against your own subscription, or against your own API key if you choose one. Pyloxa never resells or proxies any AI service.
faq-title.6: What do I need to install?
faq-title.7: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), git, and at least one of Claude Code or Codex CLI, signed in. Gemini CLI is optional and experimental, and needs your own paid Gemini API key. With more than one CLI, the default flow splits the work and fallback becomes useful. Don't have them yet? On first launch, the setup wizard checks for git and Node.js, installs the CLIs with their official npm commands after you confirm, and walks you through sign-in and API keys.
faq-title.9: Never. It checks sign-in status with each CLI’s own command and starts the CLI as you would. Tokens and credential files are not read, copied or sent.
faq-title.11: The free version needs no account, and Pyloxa never sends us your projects, prompts or code; your code goes only where the CLIs send it, under Anthropic’s, OpenAI’s and Google’s terms. The trial, the Pro preview and Pro need you to sign in, and the account is used only for licensing: once signed in, Pyloxa refreshes its license about once a day, sending only a device ID and the app and Windows versions. Pyloxa asks GitHub for the latest Pyloxa version and its CLI compatibility catalog at startup and every 12 hours, with no project or usage data; you can turn this off in Settings. Usage statistics are computed on your computer and are sent only if you turn on anonymous sharing, which is off by default, and then contain only counts and categories. Pro notifications you set up go straight from your computer to the Telegram, Discord or webhook you choose. Details are in the privacy policy.
faq-title.12: Can an agent break my repository?
faq-title.13: Agents work in separate git worktrees, away from the working directory you are editing, and Pyloxa never stashes, resets or checks it out. When a task finishes, its changed files are checked against the write scope the plan allows, and you can review each file in the built-in diff view. Nothing is merged or pushed until you choose to.
faq-title.14: Why does Windows warn me when installing?
faq-title.15: The free installer is not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may say it protected your PC. Choose More info, then Run anyway. You can compare the installer’s SHA-256 with the one on the release page first.
faq-title.20: How is this different from tools that put agent terminals side by side?
faq-title.21: Terminal multiplexers put several agent terminals in one window so you can see which are working and which are waiting for you; some keep agents running even after you quit the app or reach remote machines. Pyloxa handles what happens outside the terminals: the brain splits the request into tasks, your rules route them, your commands check the results, a fallback is proposed when quota runs out, and you merge at the end. Pyloxa keeps working in the system tray when you close its window, and tasks interrupted by a restart can be resumed. If you want to watch every terminal yourself, a multiplexer fits; if you want to hand over a request and get checked results back, Pyloxa fits.
faq-title.22: I already pay for Claude or ChatGPT. Why not just run the CLI in a terminal?
faq-title.23: Running the CLI directly is fine, and Pyloxa uses the same CLI and the same subscription. The difference is three things: when quota runs out, Pyloxa proposes a fallback from your rules and, once you confirm, another CLI continues from the files already changed; an agent saying it is done does not count until your verification commands pass; and routing rules plus the skills each CLI can see are in one place instead of in each CLI's own settings.
faq-title.24: How is this different from a CLI's own subagents?
faq-title.25: Subagents split work inside one CLI. Pyloxa splits work across CLIs: tasks can go to different CLIs, each runs in its own worktree, your commands check the results, and another CLI takes over when one runs out of quota. You can use both together.
faq-title.26: Does it support Gemini or other agents?
faq-title.27: Since 0.1.2, Gemini CLI is supported as an experimental option with your own paid Gemini API key. Google account sign-in and AI Pro or Ultra subscriptions are not supported. Gemini can run tasks such as writing and docs but can’t be the brain or test another agent’s work, and in unattended mode it can edit files but not run commands. Other agents are being evaluated.
faq-title.31: Several projects working at once, with everything waiting on you in the task center; automatic decisions within limits you set (auto mode); automatic fallback when quota runs out; automatic cross-testing; a backup brain; saved workflows, a different one for each project, and workflows drafted from one sentence; project priority, per-connection quotas and scheduled plans; a usage dashboard and reports; notifications to Telegram, Discord or a webhook; a skills library and dispatch packs; and Agent Teams, still experimental. Pro is US$79 a year and is in a preview now: sign in to use it for free until Pro goes on sale, with at least 30 days’ notice. The early-bird price is US$49 a year, and it stays US$49 for as long as you stay subscribed. If you stop, Pro keeps working on every version released while you subscribed. The free version stays free.

wf.title: One workflow, five stages
wf.lede: The Workflow page in the app shows the whole flow at once: who plans, which phases, who does each kind of work, how it’s checked, and how it’s delivered. Every stage is your setting; the brain only proposes plans and can’t change them.
wf.tabs: The five stages of a workflow
wf.plan.h: Planning: who’s the brain, and how much you let go
wf.plan.li: If the brain is unavailable, Pro can hand planning to a backup brain. The brain never reviews work it did itself.
wf.phases.h: Phases: the brain lays them out, or you set them
wf.phases.li: Agent Teams (experimental, Pro): running agents can see the whole team’s tasks, report progress, and stop to ask you when they’re missing information.
wf.phases.m8: Waits for your approval when done
wf.assign.h: Division of work: one table decides who does what
wf.assign.p: Each row of the assignment table is one kind of work. Pick the agent it goes to first and the one that takes over; a cell left empty means that agent never gets it.
wf.assign.li: Rules for one project or one phase live in the rule list and take priority over the table.
wf.assign.m.title: Assignment table
wf.assign.m.hint: Mockup: click a cell to switch between primary, fallback and not assigned
wf.check.h: Checks: an agent saying it’s done doesn’t count
wf.check.p: Pyloxa runs the verification commands you approved in the task’s own worktree, and the task counts as done only when they pass. If they fail, the agent gets one automatic attempt to fix it.
wf.deliver.h: Delivery: you decide what’s merged and pushed
wf.deliver.p: Each task finishes in its own git worktree and is checked against its write scope before it’s merged into the integration branch. Merging into your branch, pushing, and opening a PR all wait for you.
wf.deliver.li1: When a task changes files that steer agents and automation, such as .github, .claude or CLAUDE.md, it’s never accepted automatically, and the merge dialog lists those files again.
wf.deliver.li3: Pyloxa never runs stash, reset or checkout on your working directory.
wf.deliver.m4: Append Pyloxa’s verification card to the description (3 results)
wf.tpl.h: Start from one of five templates
wf.tpl.p: Before you apply one, Pyloxa lists every setting it changes, and “Undo last template” takes you back. Pro settings in a template are skipped in the free version.
wf.tpl.d1: Frontend to Claude Code, backend to Codex, each the other’s fallback; suggest, then ask.
wf.tpl.d2: Runs by your settings only, in one shared worktree, all on the brain’s profile.
wf.tpl.d3: The brain reviews every task, and frontend and backend work is cross-tested.
wf.tpl.d4: Spreads each kind of work across Claude Code and Codex, with automatic fallback when quota runs out.
fq.p2: The title bar shows how much of your Claude Code subscription is left: yellow at 70% used, red at 90% or when you’re limited. Codex and other connections show today’s tokens and are flagged when limited.
fq.card: Claude Code can take over and continue from what Codex finished, or Codex can retry after its quota resets.
fq.pro: Pro takes over automatically along the fallback chain in your rules, without asking each time; at most 2 takeovers per task.
mem.title: Every agent reads the same context
mem.p: Write down your project’s rules, conventions and pitfalls once, and Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI all read them. Skills work the same way: one place to manage them instead of a copy in every CLI.
mem.s1d: Press “Remember” on a brain reply or in a task session, or pick entries to import from CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and the other CLIs’ memory files.
mem.s2d: While they work, agents can search memory and suggest new entries. No agent sees a suggestion until you accept it, unless you let a project accept the facts and pitfalls agents suggest automatically (off by default).
mem.s3d: Write the project’s rules into a Pyloxa block in AGENTS.md, so the CLIs read them in your terminal too. You see the diff first, and nothing is committed for you.
mem.s5d: One skills library synced to every CLI and assigned per project or profile, and packed with your rules and command suggestions into a dispatch pack to share.

wf.mine.h: Save your own workflows, one per project
wf.mine.p: Once it’s set up, choose “Save as my workflow”, then pick a workflow for each project: spec first for the API, straight edits for a small tool. Or describe the way you want to work in one sentence and let the brain draft the workflow.
wf.mine.li1: The brain only drafts. Phases, assignments and checks are shown as a diff first, and you choose whether to apply it globally, save it as one of your workflows, or edit the description and draft again.

wf.mine.li3: Applying globally saves your current settings first, so you can undo it. Projects without a workflow of their own use the global settings.

td.title: Take a test drive on a sample project
td.lede: Your first run doesn’t have to risk your own project. On the last step of the setup wizard, choose “Start the test drive”: Pyloxa creates a small shopping-cart repo and asks an agent to add a feature. A rounding bug is hidden in it on purpose.
td.s1: The plan is written in advance, so it doesn’t go through the brain or use the brain’s quota, and it still waits for your approval.
td.s2: One agent builds the feature, and Pyloxa runs the test command itself instead of taking the agent’s word for it.
td.s3: An agent from another vendor adds tests from the spec and sends the work back if it finds the bug. Pro cross-tests automatically; in the free version you choose “Have another agent test it”.
td.s4: After you accept the result, open “Verification card” under the plan card to see which checks actually ran at each step.
td.note: Needs git and Node.js. With only one agent, a spec test included in the repo does the checking. Before it starts, Pyloxa shows who builds, who tests, and an estimate of agent turns, tokens and time. The test drive never touches your projects, pushes or opens a PR.

faq.td.q: Can I try it without using my own project?
faq.td.a: Yes. On the last step of the setup wizard, or on the welcome page before you have any projects, choose “Start the test drive”. Pyloxa creates a shopping-cart sample repo with a hidden bug and a plan written in advance, and waits for your approval. With CLIs from two vendors, one builds and the other cross-tests; with only one, a spec test included in the repo does the checking. Pyloxa runs the tests itself, and you can open the verification card at the end. Before it starts, you see an estimate of agent turns, tokens and time. The test drive never touches your projects, pushes or opens a PR.
faq.move.q: Do I have to set everything up again on a new PC?
faq.move.a: No. Export your settings in Settings → Backup and transfer and import them on the new PC: agent profiles, global routing rules, routing and brain preferences, stages, prompt templates, global shared memory, the skills library and interface preferences travel in one file. API keys, sign-ins, licenses and paths on this PC are never included. Per-project settings and saved workflows stay behind too; project rules can live in the repo’s .pyloxa/ folder and travel with git. You preview each item before importing, this PC’s settings are backed up automatically first, and you can restore them. It’s in the free version.
